stem: What is meant by power of accommodation of the eye?
solution:
The **power of accommodation** is the ability of the eye to adjust the focal length of its lens so that it can focus clearly on objects at different distances.

The eye lens is made of a flexible material, and the **ciliary muscles** change its curvature:

- To look at a **distant** object the ciliary muscles relax, the lens becomes thin, its focal length increases, and the distant object is focussed on the retina.
- To look at a **nearby** object the ciliary muscles contract, the lens becomes thicker, its focal length decreases, and the near object is focussed on the retina.

There is a limit to this: the focal length cannot be decreased below a certain minimum, which is why a normal eye cannot focus on an object closer than about 25 cm.
groundedIn: §10.1.1 Power of Accommodation — the ciliary muscles change the curvature and hence the focal length of the eye lens.

subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
stem: A person with a myopic eye cannot see objects beyond 1.2 m distinctly. What should be the type of the corrective lens used to restore proper vision?
solution:
The person needs a **concave (diverging) lens**.

In myopia the far point has come closer than infinity — here it is 1.2 m. A concave lens of suitable power diverges the rays from a distant object so that they appear to come from the person's own far point, 1.2 m away, from where the eye can focus them on the retina.

The required focal length is the negative of the far-point distance:

\(f = -1.2\,\text{m}\), so \(P = \dfrac{1}{f} = -0.83\,\text{D}\)
groundedIn: §10.2 Defects of Vision and their Correction — myopia is corrected by using a concave lens of suitable power.

stem: What is the far point and near point of the human eye with normal vision?
solution:
- The **far point** of a normal eye is at **infinity**. It is the farthest point up to which the eye can see objects clearly.
- The **near point** of a normal eye is about **25 cm**. It is the closest point at which the eye can see an object clearly and without strain, and it is also called the least distance of distinct vision.

A normal eye can therefore see everything from 25 cm to infinity distinctly. (For a young child the near point can be as close as about 7 to 8 cm.)
groundedIn: §10.1.1 — 'The minimum distance, at which objects can be seen most distinctly without strain, is called the least distance of distinct vision... about 25 cm' for a young adult with normal vision.

subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
stem: A student has difficulty reading the blackboard while sitting in the last row. What could be the defect the child is suffering from? How can it be corrected?
solution:
The child is suffering from **myopia**, or short-sightedness. A myopic eye can see nearby objects clearly but not distant ones, because the image of a distant object is formed **in front of** the retina rather than on it — either the eyeball has become too long or the eye lens has too short a focal length.

It is corrected by using **spectacles with a concave lens** of suitable power. The concave lens diverges the incoming rays just enough that the eye then brings them to a focus on the retina, and the blackboard becomes clear.
groundedIn: §10.2 — myopia, its two causes, and its correction with a concave lens of suitable power.
